question_text: A shipbuilder based in South Korea has signed a contract with a Norwegian owner on 14 March 2024 to construct a series of three identical 180-metre general cargo vessels, hull numbers 701, 702, and 703. The builder intends to seek DNV class for all three vessels. Six months after signing, the owner exercises an option to add a fourth vessel, hull number 704, to the series. The builder's quality management system documentation and asbestos-free declarations are on file with the Society. For the main structural welding, the builder plans to use a subcontracted welding shop that has not previously worked on DNV-classed projects. The builder asks whether hull 704 can be classed under the same rules version that applies to hulls 701–703, and what obligations the builder must meet regarding the subcontracted welding shop before classification surveys can proceed.
required_facts: Hull 704 qualifies as part of the same series because the option was exercised within 1 year of the original contract signing (6 months < 1 year limit).
The date of 'contract for construction' for hull 704 is the same as for hulls 701–703 (14 March 2024), so the same rule edition applies to all four vessels.
The subcontracted welding shop must be approved by the Society before it can perform welding of important structures on any of the vessels.
Welding must be carried out by approved welders using approved welding consumables and following approved welding procedures.
The builder retains full responsibility for integration of systems and subcontracted work, and must ensure proper interaction between all involved parties.
The builder must instruct subcontractors that the Society's rules apply and that the Society's certificates shall be provided as required.

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Sec4 [1.2.1] directs that manufacturers not covered by Sec2 [1.2] shall be considered for approval; Sec2 [1.3.2] defines the 'contract for construction' date rules including the one-year option window for series vessels, which determines which rule edition applies to hull 704.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — The question about hull 704's applicable rules requires understanding the 'contract for construction' date. Sec4 references Sec2 for manufacturer/builder requirements. Step 2 — Sec2 [1.3.2] clause 2 states that optional vessels are part of the same series if the option is exercised not later than 1 year after the contract to build the series was signed. The option for hull 704 was exercised 6 months after the original contract (14 March 2024), which is within the 1-year window. Therefore hull 704 shares the same contract for construction date as hulls 701–703 and the same rule edition applies. Step 3 — Sec2 [1.2.4] requires that welding of important structures be carried out by approved welders, with approved welding consumables, following approved welding procedures, and at welding shops approved by the Society. The subcontracted welding shop must therefore be approved by the Society before classification surveys can proceed. Step 4 — Sec4 [1.2.1] further requires that manufacturers of materials, components and systems not covered by Sec2 [1.2] be considered for approval according to criteria established by the Society.

question_text: A bulk carrier with a breadth B = 36 m, block coefficient C_B = 0.82, and scantling draught T_SC = 14.5 m is being assessed for strength. The vessel has bilge keels fitted and a metacentric height GM = 0.07 B. The loading condition under review has a draught T_LC = 11.6 m amidships. A designer needs to determine the roll period T_θ and the roll angle θ to be used in the strength assessment for the extreme sea loads design load scenario. The vessel has no service restriction notation. Calculate T_θ (in seconds) and θ (in degrees), and confirm which dynamic load combination factors apply to the roll-induced transverse acceleration component (C_YR) for the BSR load case during strength assessment.
required_facts: T_θ ≈ 20.4 s (roll period computed from Sec.3 [2.1.1] formula using k_r = 0.39B and GM = 0.07B)
θ ≈ 20.4 deg (roll angle for strength assessment with f_ps = 1.0 and f_BK = 1.0 for bilge-keel-fitted vessel)
f_BK = 1.0 applies because the vessel has bilge keels fitted
f_ps = 1.0 applies for the extreme sea loads design load scenario with no service restriction (R0 notation)
The dynamic load combination factors for strength assessment, including C_YR for the BSR load case, are found in Sec.2 [2] as directed by Sec.1 [1.1.5]
C_YR = ±1 for the BSR load case, meaning the full roll-induced transverse acceleration component is applied
The roll motion parameters (T_θ and θ) defined in Sec.3 [2.1.1] feed directly into the acceleration components referenced in the Sec.2 load combination factor tables

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Sec.1 [1.1.5] directs the reader to Sec.2 [2] for the EDWs and dynamic load combination factors for strength assessment; Sec.2 [2] defines the load combination factors (including C_YR for BSR) and references Sec.3 for the acceleration components; Sec.3 [2.1.1] provides the roll period and roll angle formulae needed to compute the actual motion values.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation:
Step 1 — Sec.1 [1.1.5]: For strength assessment, the EDWs and dynamic load combination factors for global loads are listed in Sec.2 [2]. This directs the reader to Sec.2.

Step 2 — Sec.2 [2]: The BSR (beam sea roll) load case table lists C_YR = -1 (or +1 depending on sub-case) for the transverse acceleration due to roll. Sec.2 also references Sec.3 for the definitions of the acceleration components a_roll-y, etc.

Step 3 — Sec.3 [2.1.1]: Roll period formula: T_θ = (2.3π k_r) / sqrt(g · GM). With B = 36 m, k_r = 0.39 B = 0.39 × 36 = 14.04 m (ship with bilge keel, general formula), GM = 0.07 × 36 = 2.52 m, g = 9.81 m/s²: T_θ = (2.3π × 14.04) / sqrt(9.81 × 2.52) = (101.44) / sqrt(24.72) = 101.44 / 4.972 ≈ 20.4 s.

Roll angle formula: θ = [9000 × (1.4 − 0.035 T_θ) × f_p × f_BK] / [(1.15 B + 55) π]. For strength assessment, f_p = f_ps = 1.0 (extreme sea loads, no service restriction, R0). f_BK = 1.0 (bilge keels fitted). θ = [9000 × (1.4 − 0.035 × 20.4) × 1.0 × 1.0] / [(1.15 × 36 + 55) × π] = [9000 × (1.4 − 0.714)] / [(41.4 + 55) × π] = [9000 × 0.686] / [96.4 × π] = 6174 / 302.9 ≈ 20.4 deg.

For the BSR load case, C_YR = -1 (weather side) or +1 depending on sign convention in the load case table in Sec.2 [2], meaning the full roll-induced transverse acceleration is applied without reduction.

question_text: A 95-metre general cargo vessel is being designed with a bow anchor windlass fitted on the exposed forecastle deck. The forecastle deck height above the summer load waterline is 4.8 m, and the windlass is located 18 m aft of the forward perpendicular. The anchor chain cable has a minimum breaking strength (BS) of 1 150 kN. A chain stopper is installed alongside the windlass. The windlass foundation is a fabricated steel pedestal welded to the forecastle deck, not selected from any accepted industry standard. During the design review, the structural engineer proposes to assess the foundation strength using beam theory only, and sets the permissible normal stress equal to 0.85 R_eH. The chain stopper is rated to take the full holding load during anchoring. (1) What design load, in kN, must the windlass foundation be designed for during anchoring operations, given that a chain stopper is provided? (2) Is the proposed permissible normal stress of 0.85 R_eH acceptable for a beam-theory strength assessment? (3) What minimum corrosion addition t_c applies to the fabricated pedestal foundation? (4) Does the green sea load requirement apply to this windlass installation, and why?
required_facts: Windlass foundation anchoring design load = 45% × 1150 kN = 517.5 kN (because chain stopper is provided)
Chain stopper design load = 80% × 1150 kN = 920 kN
Permissible normal stress for beam-theory assessment = 1.0 R_eH; the proposed 0.85 R_eH is within the allowable limit
Minimum corrosion addition t_c = 2.0 mm for the fabricated pedestal foundation not from an accepted industry standard
Green sea load requirement applies: ship length 95 m ≥ 80 m, deck height 4.8 m < 9.5 m (= 0.1 × 95 m) threshold, and windlass is within forward 0.25L (18 m < 23.75 m)

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Sec2 [2.1] states the windlass/chain stopper subsection applies to foundations required in accordance with Sec1 Table 2 (cross-reference within same chapter). Sec2 [2.3.1] gives the anchoring load fractions. Sec2 [2.4.2] gives permissible stresses for beam theory. Sec2 [2.5.1] sets the green sea applicability threshold. Sec2 [5.8.1] gives corrosion addition for non-standard pedestals.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Anchoring design load: Per Sec2 [2.3.1](a), when a chain stopper is provided, the windlass design load is 45% of BS = 0.45 × 1150 = 517.5 kN. The chain stopper itself must be designed for 80% of BS = 920 kN per [2.3.1](c), but the question asks about the windlass foundation load. Step 2 — Permissible normal stress: Per Sec2 [2.4.2](a), for beam theory the permissible normal stress is 1.0 R_eH (not 0.85 R_eH). The proposed value of 0.85 R_eH is more conservative than required but the rule sets the limit at 1.0 R_eH; however the key point is that 0.85 R_eH is below the rule limit so it is acceptable from a compliance standpoint — but the engineer should be aware the rule allows up to 1.0 R_eH. Actually re-reading: the rule states normal stress = 1.0 R_eH as the permissible limit, so 0.85 R_eH is within the limit and acceptable. Step 3 — Corrosion addition: Per Sec2 [5.8.1], for pedestals and foundations on deck not part of a fitting from an accepted industry standard, t_c ≥ 2.0 mm. Step 4 — Green sea applicability: Per Sec2 [2.5.1], the green sea requirement applies to windlasses on exposed decks over the forward 0.25L of ships of length 80 m or more, where the deck height is less than 0.1L or 22 m above the summer load waterline, whichever is lesser. For this ship: L = 95 m, so 0.1L = 9.5 m; lesser of 9.5 m and 22 m is 9.5 m. Deck height = 4.8 m < 9.5 m threshold. Windlass is at 18 m aft of FP, and 0.25L = 23.75 m, so 18 m < 23.75 m — within forward 0.25L. Ship length 95 m ≥ 80 m. All three conditions are met, so the green sea load requirement DOES apply. The cross-reference to Sec1 is triggered by Sec2 [2.1] which states the subsection applies to windlasses 'required to be installed in accordance with Sec.1 Table 2', meaning the answerer must consult Sec1 to confirm the windlass installation requirement before applying Sec2 scantling rules.

question_text: A RO/RO ferry has a stern door with a light opening area of 8 m² leading to the RO/RO vehicle deck. The door is located below the freeboard deck and, according to the approved damage stability calculations, the lower edge of the door opening sits 1.4 m below the most unfavourable damage waterplane at that location. The door is 3.2 m wide × 2.5 m tall, opens inwards, and weighs 4.2 tonnes. The total packing force is 18 kN. During the design review, the shipyard proposes to verify structural adequacy of the door using only a structural finite element analysis, without performing any physical pressure test on the door itself. Is this proposal acceptable under classification rules? If a physical pressure test is required, what minimum hydrostatic head must be applied, and to what acceptance criterion must the door be tested?
required_facts: The door becomes immersed in the damaged condition and must therefore be subjected to a hydrostatic pressure test per the damage condition testing requirement
The minimum hydrostatic head for the pressure test is 1.4 m, measured from the lower edge of the door opening to the most unfavourable damage waterplane
The acceptance criterion for the hydrostatic pressure test is no leakage
Because the door area (8 m²) exceeds 6 m², structural analysis may be accepted in lieu of pressure testing for structural adequacy
If gasket seals are used, a prototype pressure test of the gasket seal is still required even when structural analysis substitutes for the full pressure test
After installation, the initial gasket compression must be documented

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: The stern door is below the freeboard deck and becomes immersed in the damage condition (Sec5 [1.2.2] requires watertightness for openings below the final damage waterline). The door area is 8 m² (< 12 m²), so securing bolts may carry sea pressure (Sec5 [1.3.4]). Because the door is immersed in the damaged condition, Sec1 [3.3.3] is triggered: doors immersed by an equilibrium or intermediate waterplane in a damaged condition must be subjected to a hydrostatic pressure test. The head of water must correspond at least to the head from the lower edge of the door opening to the most unfavourable damage waterplane. Structural analysis alone is not sufficient for the watertightness test; however, for large doors above 6 m² structural analysis may be accepted in lieu of pressure testing for structural adequacy — but the door here is 8 m² > 6 m², so structural analysis may be accepted in lieu of pressure testing. However, where gasket seals are used, a prototype pressure test of the gasket seal is still required. The acceptance criterion is no leakage.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Sec5 [1.2.2]: The door leads to a compartment assumed intact in damage analysis and is below the final damage waterline, so it must be watertight. Step 2 — Sec5 [1.3.4]: Opening area 8 m² < 12 m², so securing bolts may carry sea pressure to coamings. Step 3 — Sec1 [3.3.3]: Because the door is immersed by the damage waterplane, a hydrostatic pressure test is required. The test head = 1.4 m (from lower edge of door opening to most unfavourable damage waterplane). Acceptance criterion = no leakage. Step 4 — Sec1 [3.3.3] exception: The door area is 8 m² > 6 m², so structural analysis may be accepted in lieu of pressure testing for structural strength. However, if gasket seals are used, a prototype pressure test of the gasket seal must still be carried out to confirm gasket compression can accommodate maximum deflection from the structural analysis. After installation, initial gasket compression must be documented.

scenario_parameters.location: below freeboard deck, leading to RO/RO space
scenario_parameters.proposed_verification_method: FE structural analysis only, no physical pressure test

question_text: A 145-meter bulk carrier is being designed with transverse web frames acting as primary supporting members in the cargo hold region. At each frame, longitudinal stiffeners on the inner bottom pass through cut-outs in the transverse web frame. The designer has sized the fillet welds connecting the longitudinal stiffeners to the transverse web frames and now needs to verify the weld sizing calculation method. The web frames have a web depth of 1200 mm. The cut-outs for the longitudinal stiffeners are 480 mm deep (measured as the total depth of the cut-out opening), and no lug or collar plates are fitted at these cut-outs. The ship's length exceeds 90 meters, so the designer has opted to use the detailed calculation method rather than the simplified approach. For the weld sizing of these stiffener-to-PSM connections, the designer references a fillet weld sizing formula found in a separate chapter on welding. Identify: (1) whether the cut-out depth arrangement is compliant, (2) which calculation method applies for the weld sizing given the ship length, and (3) which specific weld sizing clause from the welding chapter must be used for this detailed calculation method — noting that the simplified method for ships under 90 m references a different sub-clause in that same welding section.
required_facts: Cut-out depth ratio is 40% (480/1200), which does not exceed the 50% limit, so the arrangement is compliant without lug or collar plates
The simplified calculation method is only applicable for ships of length less than 90 m
Because the ship is 145 m, the detailed calculation method (not the simplified method) applies for the stiffener-to-PSM connection
For the detailed method, fillet weld sizing must be calculated according to Ch.13 Sec.1 [2.5.6]
The simplified method references Ch.13 Sec.1 [2.5.4], which is a different sub-clause and does not apply here

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Pt3.Ch6.Sec7 [1.2.8] states that fillet weld sizing for the detailed method shall be calculated according to Ch.13 Sec.1 [2.5.6]. The simplified method [1.3.4] references Ch.13 Sec.1 [2.5.4] instead. The question forces the answerer to distinguish which method applies (ship > 90 m → detailed method) and then follow the cross-reference to the correct welding sub-clause.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1: Check cut-out depth compliance per Pt3.Ch6.Sec7 [1.1.2]. Cut-out depth = 480 mm, PSM web depth = 1200 mm. Ratio = 480/1200 = 40%, which is less than 50%. No lug or collar plate is required on this basis alone — the arrangement is compliant with [1.1.2]. Step 2: Determine which connection calculation method applies. Per [1.2.1], the detailed calculation method ([1.2]) may be used irrespective of ship length. Per [1.3.1], the simplified method is only applicable for ships of length less than 90 m. Since the ship is 145 m, the simplified method is not applicable; the detailed method [1.2] must be used. Step 3: Identify the weld sizing clause. Per [1.2.8], fillet welds for the detailed method shall be calculated according to Ch.13 Sec.1 [2.5.6]. By contrast, [1.3.4] (simplified method) references Ch.13 Sec.1 [2.5.4]. The answerer must navigate from Sec.7 [1.2.8] to Ch.13 Sec.1 [2.5.6].

question_text: During the detail design review of a 180 m general cargo vessel, a structural engineer is evaluating the end bracket arrangement for a longitudinal shell stiffener in the midship region. The stiffener has an integral bracket where the flange transitions from the stiffener to the bracket. The designer has proposed curving the flange at the knuckle rather than fitting a tripping support. The stiffener flange has a free outstand of 65 mm and a net flange thickness of 12 mm. Is the proposed curved flange arrangement acceptable, and if so, what is the minimum radius of curvature required for the flange at the knuckle transition?
required_facts: The curved flange alternative is permitted by the rules as an alternative to fitting a tripping support at the knuckle of an integral bracket
The minimum radius formula is r = 1.6 × b1² / tf (in mm)
b1 is the free flange outstand as defined in the structural idealisation section, equal to 65 mm in this scenario
tf is the net flange thickness, equal to 12 mm in this scenario
The minimum required radius of curvature is approximately 563 mm
The proposed arrangement is acceptable only if the actual curved radius is not less than 563 mm

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Sec6 [2.1.2] permits curving the flange at an integral bracket knuckle as an alternative to tripping support, and gives the minimum radius formula r = 1.6 * b1^2 / tf, where b1 is the free flange outstand as defined in Sec7 [1.3.4]. The answerer must follow the cross-reference to Sec7 to correctly identify b1.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Sec6 [2.1.2] states that if the flange transition between a stiffener and an integral bracket is knuckled, the flange shall be effectively supported at the knuckle, OR alternatively the flange may be curved with a radius (in mm) not less than r = 1.6 * b1^2 / tf, referencing Sec7 Figure 15 for illustration. Step 2 — The formula parameter b1 is defined as the free flange outstand as defined in Sec7 [1.3.4]. The answerer must navigate to Sec7 [1.3.4] to confirm the correct interpretation of b1 (free flange outstand, measured from the web face to the flange tip). Step 3 — With b1 = 65 mm and tf = 12 mm, compute r = 1.6 * (65^2) / 12 = 1.6 * 4225 / 12 = 6760 / 12 ≈ 563 mm. Step 4 — The curved flange arrangement is acceptable provided the radius is not less than 563 mm.

scenario_parameters.stiffener_type: longitudinal shell stiffener with integral bracket
scenario_parameters.proposed_arrangement: curved flange at knuckle (no tripping bracket)

question_text:
A bulk carrier with the following characteristics is being assessed for internal tank loads on a ballast water tank:

- Ship length L = 180 m
- Breadth B = 32 m
- Block coefficient C_B = 0.82
- Scantling draught T_SC = 11.5 m
- Loading condition draught T_LC = 9.2 m
- Metacentric height GM = 2.8 m
- Roll radius of gyration k_r = 12.5 m (calculated value)
- Bilge keel fitted
- Service area notation R0 (unrestricted service)
- The ballast tank has its volumetric centre of gravity at coordinates x_G = 90 m, y_G = 8 m, z_G = 6 m (from the reference coordinate system)
- The load point under assessment is located at x = 90 m, y = 14 m, z = 2 m

For the dynamic inertial pressure calculation on the tank boundary at the load point, the designer needs the envelope transverse acceleration a_y-env. A junior engineer claims that the envelope transverse acceleration at this load point is simply equal to the roll-induced transverse acceleration a_roll-y, with no additional gravity component. Is this claim correct? Additionally, calculate the roll period T_θ and roll angle θ for this loading condition (strength assessment, extreme sea loads scenario), and determine the transverse acceleration due to roll a_roll-y at the load point, given that the ship's rotation centre R is at 4.625 m.
required_facts: The junior engineer's claim is incorrect — the envelope transverse acceleration a_y-env includes both the roll-induced transverse acceleration a_roll-y and a gravity component (g·sin θ), not just a_roll-y alone
The roll period T_θ ≈ 17.2 s (using T_θ = 2.3π·k_r / √(g·GM) with k_r = 12.5 m, GM = 2.8 m)
The roll angle θ ≈ 24.9 deg (using the roll angle formula with f_p = 1.0 for extreme sea loads R0, f_BK = 1.0 for bilge keel fitted)
The transverse acceleration due to roll a_roll-y at the load point depends on (z − R), where R = 4.625 m is the ship's rotation centre

The accelerations a_x-env, a_y-env, a_z-env used in the dynamic inertial pressure formula in the internal loads section are defined in the ship motions and accelerations section under the envelope accelerations subsection
f_T = T_LC / T_SC = 9.2 / 11.5 = 0.8, which is within the valid range [0.5, 1.0]

annotator_grounding.start_clause: Pt3.Ch4.Sec6 [Symbols] — definition of a_x-env, a_y-env, a_z-env referencing Sec.3 [3.2]
annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Sec.6 symbols define the envelope accelerations (a_x-env, a_y-env, a_z-env) used in the dynamic inertial pressure formula as 'defined in Sec.3 [3.2]'. The answerer must navigate to Sec.3 to find the roll period formula, roll angle formula, and the envelope transverse acceleration formula which includes both the roll transverse component and a gravity term (g·sin θ), disproving the junior engineer's claim.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation:
Step 1 — Sec.6 symbols: The accelerations a_x-env, a_y-env, a_z-env at the tank's volumetric centre of gravity are defined in Sec.3 [3.2]. This cross-reference is mandatory to evaluate the dynamic inertial pressure.

Step 2 — Navigate to Sec.3 [2.1.1] for roll period:
T_θ = (2.3π × k_r) / √(g × GM)
T_θ = (2.3π × 12.5) / √(9.81 × 2.8)
= (90.32) / √(27.468)
= 90.32 / 5.241
≈ 17.23 s

Step 3 — Roll angle (Sec.3 [2.1.1]), strength assessment, extreme sea loads, R0 service, bilge keel fitted:
f_ps = 1.0 (extreme sea loads, R0)
f_p = f_ps = 1.0
f_BK = 1.0 (bilge keel fitted)
θ = [9000 × (1.4 − 0.035 × T_θ) × f_p × f_BK] / [(1.15B + 55) × π]
= [9000 × (1.4 − 0.035 × 17.23) × 1.0 × 1.0] / [(1.15 × 32 + 55) × π]
= [9000 × (1.4 − 0.603)] / [(36.8 + 55) × π]
= [9000 × 0.797] / [91.8 × π]
= 7173 / 288.4
≈ 24.87 deg

Step 4 — Roll acceleration (Sec.3 [3.2] or [3.3.2]):
a_roll = (π/T_θ)² × θ × (π/180) — this is the angular acceleration amplitude; the transverse acceleration due to roll at a point is:
a_roll-y = a_roll × (z − R)
where a_roll = (2π/T_θ)² × θ_rad × ... 
More precisely from Sec.3 [3.3.2]: a_roll-y = a_roll × (z − R)
with a_roll (angular) = (2π/T_θ)² × (θ × π/180) ... but the standard DNV formula gives:
a_roll = (π × θ) / (T_θ × 180) × (2π/T_θ) ... 
Using the standard form: a_roll-y = a_roll(z − R) where a_roll = (2π/T_θ)² × (θ_rad)
θ_rad = 24.87 × π/180 = 0.4341 rad
a_roll = (2π/17.23)² × 0.4341 = (0.3648)² × 0.4341 = 0.1331 × 0.4341 ≈ 0.0578 rad/s²
a_roll-y = 0.0578 × (z − R) = 0.0578 × (2 − 4.625) = 0.0578 × (−2.625) ≈ −0.152 m/s² (magnitude 0.152 m/s²)

Step 5 — Envelope transverse acceleration (Sec.3 [3.3.2]):
The envelope transverse acceleration includes both the roll-induced transverse acceleration AND a gravity component: a_y-env = a_roll-y + g × sin(θ). The junior engineer's claim is INCORRECT — the gravity component g·sin(θ) must be added. This is the key cross-reference finding from Sec.3 [3.3.2].

question_text:
A shipowner wants to register a 78-meter vessel that operates as a floating marine biology laboratory, conducting water sampling, specimen collection, and underwater drone deployments in coastal waters. The vessel has no cargo-carrying function, no dynamic positioning system, and no special propulsion arrangement. The owner requests that the classification society formally recognize the vessel's unique purpose in its class certificate. The society's surveyor notes that no existing ship type notation in the rules covers this vessel's function.

The owner asks: (1) Can the vessel's purpose be formally recognized in the class certificate, and if so, how will it appear? (2) Are there any class requirements that must be satisfied specifically as a result of this recognition? (3) If the owner later decides to install a dynamic positioning system and requests the corresponding additional class notation, where in the rules would the requirements for that notation be found?
required_facts: The vessel qualifies for a descriptive notation because its purpose is not covered by any existing ship type notation
The descriptive notation is assigned upon request to the Society
The descriptive notation appears in square brackets on the class certificate, e.g. [Marine biology laboratory]
There are no class requirements associated with a descriptive notation
DYNPOS is an additional class notation listed in the additional class notations section (Sec.4), with design requirements found in Pt.6

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Sec.7 governs descriptive notations for vessels whose purpose is not covered by existing notations; Sec.7 [1.3] explicitly states there are no class requirements associated with a descriptive notation. The changes history in Sec.7 references Sec.4 for additional class notations including DYNPOS qualifiers, and Sec.4 [1.1.1] directs to Pt.6 for the actual design requirements of additional class notations such as DYNPOS.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — The surveyor consults the descriptive notation rules (Sec.7). Sec.7 [1.1] confirms that a vessel whose purpose or function is not covered by existing notations may have that purpose recognized by assignment of a descriptive notation. question_text: A 95-metre general cargo vessel has an internal watertight hatch located in a non-collision bulkhead. The hatch cover plate is stiffened with flat bar stiffeners (not laterally loaded, not on tight floors) with a web depth of 220 mm and a net web thickness of 8 mm. The designer claims the stiffener web plate proportions are acceptable. Is this claim correct, and what is the minimum net web thickness required for these flat bar stiffeners?
required_facts: The slenderness requirement for stiffener web plates applies to hatch stiffeners via the cross-reference to Ch.8 Sec.2
For flat bar stiffeners (standard case), the slenderness coefficient C_w = 22
The minimum net web thickness formula is t_w ≥ (h_w / C_w) × sqrt(R_eH / 235)
For h_w = 220 mm, C_w = 22, and R_eH = 235 N/mm², the minimum t_w = 10.0 mm
The proposed web thickness of 8 mm is less than the required 10 mm
The designer's claim is incorrect — the stiffener web plate does not comply

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Pt3.Ch12.Sec3 [4.3.2] specifies that plates and stiffeners of internal watertight doors/hatches shall fulfil requirements of Ch.6 Sec.4 and Ch.6 Sec.5 respectively. However, [4.3.2] also cross-references slenderness requirements; the stiffener proportions for the hatch must comply with Ch.8 Sec.2 [3.1.1], which gives the slenderness criterion for stiffener web plates including the Cw coefficient for flat bars.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Pt3.Ch12.Sec3 [4.3.2]: Internal watertight hatch stiffeners must satisfy the requirements for stiffeners (Ch.6 Sec.5). Stiffener scantlings must also comply with slenderness requirements. Step 2 — Pt3.Ch8.Sec2 [3.1.1a]: The net web thickness of a stiffener must satisfy t_w ≥ (h_w / C_w) × sqrt(R_eH / 235). Step 3 — Table 2 of Ch.8 Sec.2: For flat bar stiffeners (standard case, not laterally loaded, not on tight floors), C_w = 22. Step 4 — Assuming mild steel R_eH = 235 N/mm², the sqrt factor = 1.0. Step 5 — Minimum t_w = 220 / 22 × 1.0 = 10.0 mm. Step 6 — The proposed 8 mm web thickness is less than the required 10 mm, so the designer's claim is incorrect.

question_text: A RO/RO ferry has a stern door that also serves as a vehicle ramp. The door opens inwards and leads directly to an enclosed RO/RO space. The door has a light opening area of 18 m² and a mass of 8 tonnes. The deepest equilibrium waterline in the damaged condition is 1.4 m above the load calculation point of the door. The total packing force is 12 kN. The door frame is supported by two vertical primary supporting members (web frames) on either side of the opening, each spanning 2.8 m between deck and stringer with simple support at both ends and uniform lateral pressure loading. The design pressure on these web frames is 28 kN/m², the tributary breadth is 0.9 m, and the steel yield strength ReH is 315 N/mm². The designer proposes web frames with a net section modulus of 480 cm³ each. Is the proposed section modulus for the web frames sufficient, and what is the minimum required section modulus?
required_facts: The door opens inwards and leads to an enclosed RO/RO space, so the F1 formula applies: F1 = A·Pe + Fp
The web frames as surrounding structure must be checked using the primary supporting member section modulus formula Z = 1000|P|Sℓbdg²/(fbdg·Cs·ReH)
For a simply supported beam under uniform load (load model A), fbdg = 24.0 at midspan
The proposed section modulus of 480 cm³ exceeds the minimum requirement and is therefore sufficient

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Pt3.Ch12.Sec5 [1.4.3] gives the design force F1 for securing devices and surrounding structure of stern doors leading to RO/RO spaces opening inwards; the surrounding structure (web frames) must then be sized using the primary supporting member scantling formula in Pt3.Ch6.Sec6 [2.1.1].
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation:
Step 1 — Identify applicable design load formula (Pt3.Ch12.Sec5 [1.4.3]): The door opens inwards and leads to an enclosed RO/RO space, so F1 = A·Pe + Fp applies. Pe = 10·hb = 10×1.4 = 14 kN/m². F1 = 18×14 + 12 = 252 + 12 = 264 kN. This establishes the design force on the surrounding structure.

Step 2 — Determine design pressure on surrounding web frames: The web frames are the 'surrounding structure' referenced in [1.4.3]. The design pressure for the web frames is given directly in the scenario as 28 kN/m² (consistent with the sea pressure / damaged condition pressure acting on the door area tributary to each web frame).

Step 3 — Apply PSM section modulus formula (Pt3.Ch6.Sec6 [2.1.1]): Z = 1000 × |P| × S × ℓbdg² / (fbdg × Cs × ReH). For a simply supported beam with uniform load, load model A applies: fbdg = 24.0 at midspan. Cs = 0.85 for AC-II/AC-III (stern door surrounding structure in damage condition context). P = 28 kN/m², S = 0.9 m, ℓbdg = 2.8 m. Z = 1000 × 28 × 0.9 × 2.8² / (24.0 × 0.85 × 315) = 1000 × 28 × 0.9 × 7.84 / (6426) = 197,568 / 6426 ≈ 307 cm³.

Step 4 — Compare: Required Z ≈ 307 cm³; proposed Z = 480 cm³. The proposed section modulus exceeds the minimum requirement, so the arrangement is sufficient.

question_text: A newbuilding 180-metre general cargo vessel is being prepared for class submission. The vessel is fitted with two bower anchors, a windlass for each anchor, anchor chain stoppers, and anchor chain joining shackles. The shipyard's documentation package includes manufacturer declarations (MD) for the anchor windlass frames and brakes, but only material certificates (MC) from the manufacturer (not from the Society) for the anchor chain joining shackles. The windlass cable lifters and drums have product certificates issued by the manufacturer rather than by the Society. Is the compliance documentation package as described sufficient for class approval of the anchoring equipment, and if not, which specific items are non-compliant and what is required instead?
required_facts: The compliance documentation requirements for anchoring equipment are found by following the reference from the anchoring equipment section to Ch.1 Sec.3.
Anchor chain joining shackles require a material certificate (MC) issued by the Society, not merely by the manufacturer.
Anchor windlass cable lifters and drums require a product certificate (PC) issued by the Society; manufacturer-issued product certificates are not sufficient.
Anchor windlass brakes require an MC issued by the Society; a manufacturer declaration (MD) alone is not sufficient for the brake.
Anchor windlass frames may be documented with a manufacturer declaration (MD), so that item in the scenario is compliant.

The documentation package as described is not sufficient for class approval due to at least three non-compliant items: chain joining shackles, windlass cable lifter/drum certificates, and windlass brake certificates.

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Pt3.Ch11.Sec1 [1.2] directs the reader to Ch.1 Sec.3 for required compliance documentation. Ch.1 Sec.3 [3.1.2] and Table 2 specify exactly which compliance document types and issuing authorities are required for each anchoring equipment component.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1: Pt3.Ch11.Sec1 [1.2] states 'For required compliance documentation, see Ch.1 Sec.3.' This is the cross-chapter reference that must be followed. Step 2: Navigate to Pt3.Ch1.Sec3 [3.1.2], which states compliance documentation shall be submitted as required by Table 2. Step 3: Read Table 2 for each component in the scenario. (a) Anchor chain joining shackles: Table 2 requires MC (material certificate) issued by the Society (PC = product certificate from Society). The scenario provides MC from the manufacturer only — this is non-compliant; the certificate must be issued by the Society. (b) Anchor windlass cable lifter and drum: Table 2 lists these under 'MC Society' meaning the material certificate must be issued by the Society, and additionally a product certificate (PC) issued by the Society is required. The scenario provides product certificates from the manufacturer, not the Society — non-compliant. (c) Anchor windlass frame: Table 2 lists frame under 'MD Manufacturer' — manufacturer declaration is acceptable, so this is compliant. (d) Anchor windlass brake: Table 2 lists brake under 'MC Society' — a material certificate from the Society is required, not just a manufacturer declaration — non-compliant as described.

question_text: A 220 m bulk carrier with large deck openings is being designed with a loading manual. The designer notes that the ship will experience unsymmetrical loading conditions with respect to the ship's centre line during certain cargo operations. During the structural analysis, the midship cross-section includes a longitudinal bulkhead with vertical corrugations running the full length of the cargo hold region. The designer needs to determine: (1) whether permissible still water torsional moment limits must be included in the loading manual, and (2) when calculating the hull girder section modulus at the strength deck for this cross-section, should the vertical corrugations of the longitudinal bulkhead be included in the sectional area calculation? The corrugated bulkhead has corrugation geometry with sc = 600 mm, a = 400 mm, and c = 200 mm.
required_facts: Permissible still water torsional moment limits must be included in the loading manual for a ship with large deck openings
Vertical corrugations of the longitudinal bulkhead shall NOT be included in the hull girder transverse section for bending (section modulus calculation)
Vertical corrugations ARE effective for hull girder shear force despite being excluded from bending calculations
The shear reduction factor for the corrugated bulkhead is Cshr = sc/(a+c) = 600/(400+200) = 1.0
The torsional moment limit requirement for large-deck-opening ships is cross-referenced from the loading manual section to the hull girder strength characteristics section

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: The loading manual requirements in Pt3.Ch1.Sec5 [2.1.1] include a guidance note stating that permissible torsional still water moment limits are generally applicable for ships with large deck openings as given in Ch.5 Sec.1. This forces the answerer to navigate to Pt3.Ch5.Sec1 to find the rules on longitudinal bulkheads with vertical corrugations, specifically [2.5.1] which states vertical corrugations shall NOT be included in the hull girder transverse section for bending, and [2.5.2] which provides the shear reduction factor Cshr = sc/(a+c) for shear flow calculations.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1: The loading manual definition in Pt3.Ch1.Sec5 [2.1.1] states that permissible limits for still water torsional moments shall be included where applicable, and the guidance note explicitly states these limits are generally applicable for ships with large deck openings 'as given in Ch.5 Sec.1'. Step 2: Navigate to Pt3.Ch5.Sec1 to understand the torsional moment context and hull girder section properties. Step 3: In Pt3.Ch5.Sec1 [2.5.1], the rule states that for longitudinal bulkheads with vertical corrugations, the vertical corrugations shall NOT be included in the hull girder transverse section — they are not effective for hull girder bending, but ARE effective for hull girder shear force. Step 4: For the shear flow calculation per [2.5.2], the reduction factor is Cshr = sc/(a+c) = 600/(400+200) = 600/600 = 1.0. Step 5: Conclusion: (1) Yes, torsional moment limits must be in the loading manual for this ship with large deck openings; (2) No, the vertical corrugations must be excluded from the section modulus calculation at the strength deck.

question_text: A Type 'A' bulk carrier has continuous solid bulwarks running along the exposed weather deck. The bulwarks are 1.4 m high on average and form a well between the forecastle and the midship deckhouse. The designer proposes to cut several large rectangular openings in the lower portion of these bulwarks to serve as freeing ports, with the total freeing port area equal to 28% of the total bulwark area on each side. The bulwark length forming the well is 32 m, and the ship has standard sheer. The openings in the bulwarks are fitted with vertical bars spaced 230 mm apart rather than horizontal rails. Is the proposed arrangement compliant with the classification rules? Specifically: (1) does the freeing port area of 28% satisfy the applicable requirement for this ship type, and (2) do the vertical bars at 230 mm spacing provide acceptable crew protection equivalent to the required horizontal courses at the bulwark openings?
required_facts: Type 'A' ships with bulwarks must have a freeing port area of at least 33% of the total bulwark area (or open rails for at least half the exposed weather deck length)
The proposed freeing port area of 28% does not meet the 33% minimum requirement and is therefore non-compliant
Vertical bars or rails spaced approximately 230 mm apart are explicitly permitted as an alternative to horizontal courses for crew protection at bulwark openings
The 230 mm vertical bar spacing is acceptable and satisfies the crew protection requirement at the openings
The overall arrangement is non-compliant due to insufficient freeing port area, even though the bar spacing is acceptable

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Pt3.Ch11.Sec3 [2.1.2] requires that openings in bulwarks provide crew protection at least equivalent to the horizontal courses specified in Ch.12 Sec.10 [6.1], and also permits vertical bars at ~230 mm spacing as an alternative. Pt3.Ch11.Sec3 [2.1.3] directs to Ch.12 Sec.10 [1]–[5] for freeing port area requirements when bulwarks form wells. Ch.12 Sec.10 [6.1] specifies that Type 'A' ships with bulwarks must have open rails for at least half the length of the exposed weather deck OR a freeing port area of at least 33% of the total bulwark area.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1: The scenario involves a Type 'A' ship with bulwarks forming a well on the exposed weather deck — Pt3.Ch11.Sec3 [2.1.3] directs the designer to Ch.12 Sec.10 [1]–[5] for freeing port sizing, and [2.1.2] governs crew protection at openings. Step 2: Navigate to Ch.12 Sec.10 [6.1] (referenced by Pt3.Ch11.Sec3 [2.1.2] as the benchmark for crew protection equivalence). Ch.12 Sec.10 [6.1] states: Type 'A' ships with bulwarks shall have open rails fitted for at least half the length of the exposed weather deck OR a freeing port area of at least 33% of the total bulwark area in the lower part of the bulwarks. Step 3: The proposed freeing port area is 28%, which is less than the required 33% minimum for a Type 'A' ship. The arrangement does NOT satisfy the freeing port area requirement. Step 4: Regarding crew protection at the openings — Pt3.Ch11.Sec3 [2.1.2] explicitly permits vertical rails or bars spaced approximately 230 mm apart in lieu of horizontal rails, so the 230 mm vertical bar spacing IS acceptable as an equivalent to the horizontal courses referenced in Ch.12 Sec.10 [6.1]. Step 5: Conclusion — the arrangement is partially non-compliant: the freeing port area of 28% fails the 33% minimum required for Type 'A' ships, but the vertical bar spacing of 230 mm is acceptable for crew protection at the openings.

question_text: A general cargo vessel has a flat keel with no sheer along its entire length. On the freeboard deck, bulwarks form a well on each side of the ship. The bulwark length for this well is 24 metres, and the bulwarks have an average height of 1.4 metres. The designer proposes a freeing port area of 1.75 m² per side for this well. Is this arrangement compliant, and what is the minimum required freeing port area per side? In your working, identify any symbols or units you rely on from the general definitions applicable across the rules.
required_facts: Base freeing port area uses formula A = 0.07 × ℓb because ℓb = 24 m > 20 m, giving 1.68 m²
Bulwark height of 1.4 m exceeds 1.2 m threshold, requiring an increase of 0.004 m² per metre of well length per 0.1 m excess height; total height correction = +0.192 m²
The ship has no sheer, so the area (after height correction) must be increased by 50% per the no-sheer provision
Minimum required freeing port area per side = 2.808 m² (approximately 2.81 m²)
The proposed area of 1.75 m² per side is NOT compliant — it is less than the required minimum
The symbol L used in the cap ℓb ≤ 0.7L is defined in the general symbols section (Pt3.Ch1.Sec4), not in the freeing ports section itself, and represents the rule ship length in metres

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Freeing port area calculation in Pt3.Ch12.Sec10 uses symbol ℓb (bulwark length) and references Ch.1 Sec.4 for any symbols not defined locally. The answerer must consult Ch.1 Sec.4 to confirm the meaning and units of general symbols (e.g. L, length in metres) used in the formula, then apply the no-sheer 50% uplift from [2.1.2] and the height correction from [2.1.1].
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Identify applicable formula branch: ℓb = 24 m > 20 m, so use A = 0.07 × ℓb = 0.07 × 24 = 1.68 m². Step 2 — Height correction: bulwark average height = 1.4 m > 1.2 m, difference = 1.4 − 1.2 = 0.2 m = 2 × 0.1 m increments. Increase = 2 × 0.004 × 24 = 0.192 m². Adjusted base area = 1.68 + 0.192 = 1.872 m². Step 3 — No-sheer uplift (Pt3.Ch12.Sec10 [2.1.2]): ship has no sheer, so area is increased by 50%. Required area = 1.872 × 1.50 = 2.808 m² per side. Step 4 — Symbol grounding: the formula uses ℓb defined locally as bulwark length in m (max 0.7L). The symbol L (ship length) is not defined in Sec.10 itself; the section header states 'For symbols not defined in this section, see Ch.1 Sec.4', so the answerer must go to Pt3.Ch1.Sec4 Table 2 to confirm L is the rule length in metres. Step 5 — Compliance check: proposed area 1.75 m² < required 2.808 m² → NOT compliant.

question_text: A 310-metre bulk carrier is being designed for unrestricted worldwide service with a block coefficient of 0.82, a breadth-to-depth ratio of 1.9, and a length-to-breadth ratio of 5.1. The designer has specified a scantling draught of 18.5 m and a heavy ballast draught of 11.2 m. During a design review, the structural assessment team is evaluating the hull girder loads for the normal seagoing condition. For this condition, the team needs to confirm which load components must be combined to form the design vertical bending moment (VBM) and the design vertical shear force (VSF) acting on the hull cross-section, and whether any horizontal bending moment (HBM) component must also be included. Additionally, the team notes that the ship will occasionally perform ballast water exchange at sea — identify the correct design load scenario classification for that operation and state which hull girder load components apply to it.
required_facts: Design VBM for normal seagoing = Msw + Mwv-LC (still water bending moment combined with vertical wave bending moment for the dynamic load case)
Design VSF for normal seagoing = Qsw + Qwv-LC (still water shear force combined with vertical wave shear force for the dynamic load case)
Horizontal bending moment (HBM = Mwh-LC) must be included in the normal seagoing S+D scenario
For ballast water exchange at sea, the water ballast tank boundary load uses Pls-2 (static tank pressure during flow-through ballast water exchange)
Both scantling draught (18.5 m) and heavy ballast draught (11.2 m) must be considered as design operating draughts per the design basis requirements

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Pt3.Ch1.Sec2 establishes the design basis requirements — including that ships must be designed for specified operating draughts and that structural strength must be checked against the relevant load conditions. This leads the answerer into Pt3.Ch4.Sec7, which defines the principal design load scenarios and specifies exactly which hull girder load components (VBM, HBM, VSF, TM) apply to each scenario, including normal seagoing operations (Scenario 1: S+D) and ballast water exchange at sea (Scenario 2: S+D with specific components).
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Pt3.Ch1.Sec2 [3.1.3] states ships shall be designed to withstand environmental conditions for appropriate loading conditions, and [3.6] requires that both scantling draught and heavy ballast draught be considered as design operating draughts. This establishes that multiple load scenarios must be evaluated. Step 2 — The answerer must then navigate to Pt3.Ch4.Sec7, which is the section governing design load scenarios for strength assessment. Step 3 — Table 1 in Pt3.Ch4.Sec7 shows that for normal seagoing operations (Scenario 1, S+D), the design VBM = Msw + Mwv-LC, the design VSF = Qsw + Qwv-LC, and the HBM = Mwh-LC must also be included. Step 4 — For ballast water exchange at sea (Scenario 2, S+D), Table 1 shows VBM = Msw + Mwv-LC, VSF = Qsw + Qwv-LC, HBM = Mwh-LC, and the boundary condition for water ballast tanks uses Pls-2 (static tank pressure during flow-through ballast water exchange). The scenario is classified as a Static + Dynamic (S+D) load scenario.

question_text: A 180 m general cargo vessel (not a tanker) has a double bottom fitted throughout the cargo hold region. The ship has a moulded breadth B of 28 m. The designer proposes an inner bottom height of 1 300 mm above the keel line, measured vertically. Additionally, small drainage wells are constructed in the double bottom for hold drainage; the deepest point of these wells is 480 mm above the keel line. Assess whether (a) the proposed inner bottom height of 1 300 mm is compliant, and (b) the drainage well depth is acceptable. Show your calculations and state the minimum required double bottom height.
required_facts: The minimum required double bottom height is 1400 mm
The proposed inner bottom height of 1300 mm is less than 1400 mm and is therefore not compliant
The drainage well must be at least 500 mm or half the required double bottom height (700 mm) above the keel line, whichever is greater
The proposed well clearance of 480 mm is less than 700 mm and is therefore not compliant

annotator_grounding.start_clause: Pt3.Ch1.Sec4 [2.1] (symbols: B defined as moulded breadth)
annotator_grounding.chain_summary: The symbols section (Ch.1 Sec.4) defines B (moulded breadth) used in the double bottom height formula in Ch.2 Sec.3 [2.3]. The answerer must locate the double bottom height formula h_DB = 1000·B/20 (min 760 mm, max 2000 mm) and the drainage well rule requiring the well bottom to be not less than 500 mm or half the required double bottom height from the keel line.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Identify symbol B: From Ch.1 Sec.4 Table 2, B is the moulded breadth of the ship, here 28 m. Step 2 — Compute required h_DB per Ch.2 Sec.3 [2.3]: h_DB = 1000 × 28 / 20 = 1400 mm. Check minimum: 1400 mm > 760 mm ✓. Check maximum: 1400 mm < 2000 mm, so h_DB = 1400 mm governs. Step 3 — Compare proposed height: Proposed 1300 mm < required 1400 mm → NOT compliant. Step 4 — Drainage well check per Ch.2 Sec.3 [2.4]: The vertical distance from the bottom of the well to the keel plane must not be less than 500 mm OR half the required double bottom height = 1400/2 = 700 mm. The more restrictive of the two applicable limits is 700 mm (since 700 > 500). Proposed well depth above keel = 480 mm < 700 mm → NOT compliant.

question_text: A 185-metre container ship is being designed to carry containers on the weather deck, with the forward-most container stack positioned 24 metres aft of the forward perpendicular. The ship has a breadth of 28 metres. A transverse watertight boundary plate separates a ballast water tank from an adjacent dry cargo hold. The plate panel has a length of 900 mm and a breadth of 600 mm. The design pressure for the governing load set is 85 kN/m², the hull girder longitudinal stress at the load calculation point is 60 N/mm², and the material yield stress ReH is 235 N/mm². The plate is transversely stiffened and forms a transverse boundary between a ballast water tank and a dry cargo hold. Determine the minimum required net thickness of this plate panel, and state whether the arrangement satisfies the applicable acceptance criteria.
required_facts: The applicable formula for net plate thickness is t = 0.0158 × αp × b × sqrt(|P| / (Ca × ReH))
The plate falls under AC-III as a transverse boundary between a ballast water tank and a dry cargo hold not intended to carry liquid or bulk cargo
For AC-III transverse boundaries of ballast water tanks with transverse stiffening: βa = 1.30, αa = 0.00, Ca-max = 1.30
Ca = 1.30 (since αa = 0.00, the hull girder stress term vanishes)
The panel aspect ratio correction factor αp = 0.883 (calculated as 1.2 − 600/(2.1 × 900), capped at 1.0)
The minimum required net thickness is approximately 4.4 mm

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Pt5.Ch2.Sec5 [2.1] directs that net thickness of plating subjected to lateral pressure shall be derived as defined in Pt3.Ch6.Sec4 [1.1.1], using the Ca coefficients from the Pt5 table rather than the Pt3 table. The answerer must navigate from the container ship hull local scantlings section to the general plating formula in Pt3.
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation: Step 1 — Identify ship type and applicable part: 185 m container ship → Pt.5 Ch.2 applies for container ships. Step 2 — Identify the structural member: transverse watertight boundary between a ballast water tank and a dry cargo hold, transversely stiffened plating. Step 3 — Navigate to Pt5.Ch2.Sec5 [2.1]: hull local scantlings for plating subjected to lateral pressure direct the designer to use the formula in Pt3.Ch6.Sec4 [1.1.1] with Ca coefficients from Table 1 of Pt5.Ch2.Sec5. Step 4 — Determine acceptance criteria: the plate is a transverse boundary between a ballast water tank and a dry cargo hold not intended to carry liquid or bulk cargo → AC-III applies. Step 5 — Read Ca coefficients from Pt5.Ch2.Sec5 Table 1 for AC-III, transverse boundaries of ballast water tanks / transverse boundaries between tanks and dry cargo holds: βa = 1.30, αa = 0.00, Ca-max = 1.30. Step 6 — Calculate Ca: Ca = βa − αa × (σhg / ReH) = 1.30 − 0.00 × (60/235) = 1.30. Ca ≤ Ca-max = 1.30 ✓. Step 7 — Apply the formula from Pt3.Ch6.Sec4 [1.1.1]: t = 0.0158 × αp × b × sqrt(|P| / (Ca × ReH)). Step 8 — Calculate αp: αp = 1.2 − b/(2.1a) = 1.2 − 600/(2.1 × 900) = 1.2 − 0.317 = 0.883; since 0.883 < 1.0, αp = 0.883. Step 9 — Compute thickness: t = 0.0158 × 0.883 × 600 × sqrt(85 / (1.30 × 235)) = 0.0158 × 0.883 × 600 × sqrt(85 / 305.5) = 8.376 × sqrt(0.2782) = 8.376 × 0.5274 = 4.42 mm. Step 10 — Report: minimum net thickness ≈ 4.42 mm.

question_text: A 320-metre container ship is being designed with the following characteristics: length between perpendiculars L = 320 m, breadth B = 48.2 m, block coefficient CB = 0.66, waterplane coefficient CWL = 0.78, scantling draught TSC = 14.5 m. The ship can carry a maximum of 12,000 TEU of 14-tonne containers. During the structural design review, the naval architect needs to determine the vertical wave bending moments for strength assessment at the midship section (x/L = 0.5). The designer notes that the standard vertical wave bending moment formula used for general ship types is NOT applicable to this vessel, and that a ship-type-specific formula must be used instead. Using the appropriate wave bending moment formula for this vessel type, calculate: (1) the wave parameter C, (2) the hogging vertical wave bending moment MWV-Hog at x/L = 0.5, and (3) confirm the value of the factor fR that must be used for strength assessment, identifying which rule table or clause defines it. Assume the bow flare shape coefficient fBow = 0.35, the probability factor fp = 1.0, and that the reference length for vertical wave bending moments uses CWL = 0.78.
required_facts: The general vertical wave bending moment formula for standard ship types does not apply; the container-ship-specific formula from the Part 5 container ship rules must be used instead

The reference length Lref for vertical wave bending moments is approximately 435 m (using Lref = 315 × CWL^(−1.3) with CWL = 0.78), so L = 320 m < Lref and the first branch of the wave parameter formula applies
The wave parameter C ≈ 0.979
The distribution factor cM = 1.0 at x/L = 0.5 in hogging
The non-linear hogging correction fNL-Hog ≈ 0.967 (computed as 0.3 × CB/CWL × sqrt(T), not exceeding 1.1)

The factor fR for strength assessment is defined in the hull girder loads section of the general ship rules (Part 3), not in the container ship chapter itself — the answerer must follow the cross-reference to find it

annotator_grounding.chain_summary: Container ship vertical wave bending moment is defined in Pt5.Ch2.Sec3 [2.2.3], which references fR 'as given in Pt.3 Ch.4 Sec.4 [3.1.1]' for strength assessment. The symbols used (CWL, CB, etc.) are defined in Pt3.Ch1.Sec4. The answerer must: (1) recognise this is a container ship requiring Pt5 loads, (2) apply the Pt5.Ch2.Sec3 wave bending moment formula, (3) follow the fR cross-reference back to Pt3.Ch4.Sec4 [3.1.1].
annotator_grounding.expected_derivation:
Step 1 — Identify vessel type and applicable load section: The vessel is a container ship. Per Pt3.Ch4.Sec4 [1.1.3], for container ships the vertical wave bending moment defined in Pt5.Ch2 applies in lieu of the general formula. Therefore Pt5.Ch2.Sec3 [2.2] governs.
